If I could assemble a special dinner party from history, I would invite a group of brilliant, practical, and deeply thoughtful innovators. At the table, I’d seat Hypatia of Alexandria, the ancient mathematician, astronomer, and philosopher, for perspective and intellectual courage. Beside her would be Marie Curie, whose relentless scientific curiosity changed our understanding of the physical world. I’d also choose Ada Lovelace, the visionary mathematician who imagined the first computer and represented imagination meeting calculation, and Marcus Aurelius, whose philosophy offers difficult, human questions about leadership, duty, and resilience.

The conversation would be a mix of inspiration and grounded insight. I’d ask Hypatia how ancient scholars developed their understanding of the world without modern tools. Then I’d ask Marie Curie what sacrifices a personal life can tolerate for the sake of knowledge and well-being. Ada Lovelace would offer the change of asking what unseen futures might await us; perhaps she’s the only one who knows about buried algorithms. Finally, I’d ask Marcus Aurelius how to judge what you should pursue without being run over by fame, opportunity or fear.

The dinner wouldn’t be about flattery or legacy. It would be about conversation: real, precise, and sometimes difficult. The thing about visionaries like Hypatia, Curie and Lovelace is that they saw things before they existed, before they were easy to label. Aurelius would keep the conversation realistic by telling us when to withdraw, when to persue and when to take a long breath. - Maybe at some point they lovingly discuss the dinner itself, comparing the meals of the ancients and the pigeon, and Frank Franklin Franklin tells jokes about his once paper money formation.

I’d open a bok to ask them what, in their view, is harder: admission you were wrong, or knowing you were right. Hypatia would argue the first; Curie might offer the second. Ada Lovelace would say both are predictions that all minds have incomplete. Aurelius would remind you that neither one is bad if it makes a person more alive.
